title: Medicare hack claim on dark web probed
full_text:
Services Australia and law enforcement agencies are investigating claims made on the dark web by an alleged hacker offering 25 million Medicare files to the highest bidder, amid warnings from intelligence chiefs for government departments, businesses and the public to tighten cybersecurity defences.
The suspected cybercriminal posted a sample dataset of 38 files containing full names, purported Medicare card numbers and expiry dates, dates of birth, email addresses, mobile numbers and home addresses on a 150,000-member forum called Dark Forums on September 28.
Government sources said the data drop may have been an opportunistic attempt to use recycled information to cash in on the public furore following an infiltration in June of the Medicare statistics portal by a rogue OpenAI agent. The breach made national headlines and highlighted vulnerabilities within government IT systems.
The latest claims on the dark web are not linked to the OpenAI incident, which did not compromise personal information or expose it to the criminal underworld, and which is also subject to a "forensic investigation" by Services Australia and the Australian Signals Directorate.
However, both draw attention to the vulnerability of government and business IT systems and the need to upgrade cybersecurity controls to protect critical data from sophisticated cyber threats and advancing artificial intelligence.
The sample cache of 38 profiles offered by a suspected cybercriminal using the pseudonym Saotome matched digital footprints on social media sites of real individuals in Queensland, Victoria, NSW, South Australia, the ACT and Western Australia.
Services Australia, which manages the universal healthcare system, said a review found the records "contain fabricated, incorrect or mismatched Medicare card information", including "records where no corresponding Medicare record could be located".
The agency confirmed it was continuing to investigate the hacker's claims of a massive 25 million-file data leak, adding "datasets like these are often compiled from information that's become available through third-party data breaches, not our own records or systems".
"Services Australia is aware of the claims, and while we don't comment on specific cybersecurity operations, we routinely monitor and respond to threats from a range of sources," a spokesperson said.
"Where customers may be at risk following a third-party breach, we work with the National Office of Cyber Security, the Australian Cyber Security Centre and affected organisations to identify those customers and apply additional protections to their records."
The Australian Federal Police said it was aware of the incident and "liaising with the Australian Signals Directorate".
A spokesperson for Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher confirmed the minister had been informed about the potential data leak.
The suspected breach was spotted last week by a cybersecurity firm - which asked not to be publicly named because of the sensitive nature of the matter - during routine real-time threat monitoring of the dark web.
The alleged hacker was offering the files for sale via the Telegram app for $400 each set to any interested party, and the cyber firm informed the ASD.
"Unfortunately, offers like this are common and generally a routine part of the cybercrime economy," said Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst on the cyber, technology and security program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute.
"Stolen information is regularly packaged, combined with data from earlier breaches and public sources, and then traded through dark web forums and increasingly through platforms, like Telegram."
While the claims had to be tested, if they were genuine, the information could be misused by criminals for identity fraud, phishing and impersonation scams, he said.
Alastair MacGibbon, former cybersecurity adviser to Malcolm Turnbull, said any circulation of Medicare files was not necessarily a sign that Medicare systems themselves had been breached.
Information could be stolen from someone who had lawful access, or by someone misusing the database.
MacGibbon said the leaking of medical information and personal identifiable information, even in the form of "recirculated" data sets, was "never trivial" as it assisted criminals to carry out identity-style attacks.
Tom Guerin, a cyberintelligence analyst at data security firm Brighten Tech, said cyber resilience in the AI era was no longer just about keeping attackers out.
"It is about finding compromised access before attackers use it. The organisations that do that first will control the outcome," he said.
"The uncomfortable truth is that the cybersecurity model most organisations rely on is becoming obsolete. Firewalls, endpoint protection, and traditional dark web monitoring were designed for a world where attacks were slower, smaller, and largely human-driven."
